transcript.text: Hello William. This is Amber – you said to phone if I wanted to get more information about the job agency you mentioned. Is now a good time?
transcript.speaker: AMBER

transcript.text: Oh, hi Amber. Yes. Fine. So the agency I was talking about is called Bankside – they’re based in Docklands – I can tell you the address now – 497 Eastside.
transcript.speaker: WILLIAM

transcript.text: OK, thanks. So is there anyone in particular I should speak to there?
transcript.speaker: AMBER

transcript.text: The agent I always deal with is called Becky Jamieson.
transcript.speaker: WILLIAM

transcript.text: Let me write that down – Becky …
transcript.speaker: AMBER

transcript.text: Jamieson J-A-M-I-E-S-O-N.
transcript.speaker: WILLIAM

transcript.text: Do you have her direct line?
transcript.speaker: AMBER

transcript.text: Yes, it’s in my contacts somewhere – right, here we are: 078 double 6, 510 triple 3. I wouldn’t call her until the afternoon if I were you – she’s always really busy in the morning trying to fill last-minute vacancies. She’s really helpful and friendly so I’m sure it would be worth getting in touch with her for an informal chat.
transcript.speaker: WILLIAM

transcript.text: It’s mainly clerical and admin jobs they deal with, isn’t it?
transcript.speaker: AMBER

transcript.text: That’s right. I know you’re hoping to find a full-time job in the media eventually – but Becky mostly recruits temporary staff for the finance sector – which will look good on your CV – and generally pays better too.
transcript.speaker: WILLIAM

transcript.text: Yeah – I’m just a bit worried because I don’t have much office experience.
transcript.speaker: AMBER

transcript.text: I wouldn’t worry. They’ll probably start you as a receptionist, or something like that. So what’s important for that kind of job isn’t so much having business skills or knowing lots of different computer systems – it’s communication that really matters – so you’d be fine there. And you’ll pick up office skills really quickly on the job. It’s not that complicated.
transcript.speaker: WILLIAM

transcript.text: OK good. So how long do people generally need temporary staff for? It would be great if I could get something lasting at least a month.
transcript.speaker: AMBER

transcript.text: That shouldn’t be too difficult. But you’re more likely to be offered something for a week at first, which might get extended. It’s unusual to be sent somewhere for just a day or two.
transcript.speaker: WILLIAM

transcript.text: Right, I’ve heard the pay isn’t too bad – better than working in a shop or a restaurant.
transcript.speaker: AMBER

transcript.text: Oh yes – definitely. The hourly rate is about £10, 11 if you’re lucky.
transcript.speaker: WILLIAM

transcript.text: That’s pretty good. I was only expecting to get eight or nine pounds an hour.
transcript.speaker: AMBER

transcript.text: Do you want me to tell you anything about the registration process?
transcript.speaker: WILLIAM

transcript.text: Yes, please. I know you have to have an interview.
transcript.speaker: AMBER

transcript.text: The interview usually takes about an hour and you should arrange that about a week in advance.
transcript.speaker: WILLIAM

transcript.text: I suppose I should dress smartly if it’s for office work – I can probably borrow a suit from Mum.
transcript.speaker: AMBER

transcript.text: Good idea. It’s better to look too smart than too casual.
transcript.speaker: WILLIAM

transcript.text: Will I need to bring copies of my exam certificates or anything like that?
transcript.speaker: AMBER

transcript.text: No – they don’t need to see those, I don’t think.
transcript.speaker: WILLIAM

transcript.text: What about my passport?
transcript.speaker: AMBER

transcript.text: Oh yes – they will ask to see that.
transcript.speaker: WILLIAM

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: AMBER

transcript.text: I wouldn’t get stressed about the interview though. It’s just a chance for them to build a relationship with you – so they can try and match you to a job which you’ll like. So there are questions about personality that they always ask candidates – fairly basic ones. And they probably won’t ask anything too difficult like what your plans are for the future.
transcript.speaker: WILLIAM

transcript.text: Hope not.
transcript.speaker: AMBER

transcript.text: Anyway, there are lots of benefits to using an agency – for example, the interview will be useful because they’ll give you feedback on your performance so you can improve next time.
transcript.speaker: WILLIAM

transcript.text: And they’ll have access to jobs which aren’t advertised.
transcript.speaker: AMBER

transcript.text: Exactly – most temporary jobs aren’t advertised.
transcript.speaker: WILLIAM

transcript.text: And I expect finding a temporary job this way takes a lot less time – it’s much easier than ringing up individual companies.
transcript.speaker: AMBER

transcript.text: Yes indeed. Well I think …
transcript.speaker: WILLIAM

transcript.text: Good morning.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: My name’s Erica Matthews, and I’m the owner of Matthews Island Holidays, a company set up by my parents.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Thank you for coming to this presentation, in which I hope to interest you in what we have to offer.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’re a small, family-run company, and we believe in the importance of the personal touch, so we don’t aim to compete with other companies on the number of customers.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: What we do is build on our many years’ experience – more than almost any other rail holiday company – to ensure we provide perfect holidays in a small number of destinations, which we’ve got to know extremely well.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I’ll start with our six-day Isle of Man holiday.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: This is a fascinating island in the Irish Sea, with Wales to the south, England to the east, Scotland to the north and Northern Ireland to the west.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Our holiday starts in Heysham, where your tour manager will meet you, then you’ll travel by ferry to the Isle of Man.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Some people prefer to fly from Luton instead, and another popular option is to go by train to Liverpool and take a ferry from there.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: You have five nights in the hotel, and the price covers five breakfasts and dinners, and lunch on the three days when there are organised trips: day four is free, and most people have lunch in a café or restaurant in Douglas.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The price of the holiday includes the ferry to the Isle of Man, all travel on the island, the hotel, and the meals I’ve mentioned.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Incidentally, we try to make booking our holidays as simple and fair as possible, so unlike with many companies, the price is the same whether you book six months in advance or at the last minute, and there’s no supplement for single rooms in hotels.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: If you make a booking then need to change the start date, for example because of illness, you’re welcome to change to an alternative date or a different tour, for a small administrative fee.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: OK, so what does the holiday consist of?
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Well, on day one you’ll arrive in time for a short introduction by your tour manager, followed by dinner in the hotel.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The dining room looks out at the river, close to where it flows into the harbour, and there’s usually plenty of activity going on.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: On day two you’ll take the coach to the small town of Peel, on the way calling in at the Tynwald Exhibition.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The Isle of Man isn’t part of the United Kingdom, and it has its own parliament, called Tynwald.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s claimed that this is the world’s oldest parliament that’s still functioning, and that it dates back to 979.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: However, the earliest surviving reference to it is from 1422, so perhaps it isn’t quite as old as it claims!
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Day three we have a trip to the mountain Snaefell.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: This begins with a leisurely ride along the promenade in Douglas in a horse-drawn tram.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Then you board an electric train which takes you to the fishing village of Laxey.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: From there it’s an eight-kilometre ride in the Snaefell Mountain Railway to the top.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Lunch will be in the café, giving you spectacular views of the island.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Day four is free for you to explore, using the pass which we’ll give you.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: So you won’t have to pay for travel on local transport, or for entrance to the island’s heritage sites.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Or you might just want to take it easy in Douglas and perhaps do a little light shopping.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The last full day, day five, is for some people the highlight of the holiday, with a ride on the steam railway, from Douglas to Port Erin.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: After some time to explore, a coach will take you to the headland that overlooks the Calf of Man, a small island just off the coast.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: From there you continue to Castletown, which used to be the capital of the Isle of Man, and its mediaeval castle.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: And on day six it’s back to the ferry – or the airport, if you flew to the island – and time to go home.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Now I’d like to tell you …
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Ed, how are you getting on with the reading for our presentation next week?
transcript.speaker: RUTH

transcript.text: Well, OK, Ruth – but there’s so much of it.
transcript.speaker: ED

transcript.text: I know, I hadn’t realised birth order was such a popular area of research.
transcript.speaker: RUTH

transcript.text: But the stuff on birth order and personality is mostly unreliable. From what I’ve been reading a lot of claims about how your position in the family determines certain personality traits are just stereotypes, with no robust evidence to support them.
transcript.speaker: ED

transcript.text: OK, but that’s an interesting point – we could start by outlining what previous research has shown. There are studies going back over a hundred years.
transcript.speaker: RUTH

transcript.text: Yeah – so we could just run through some of the typical traits. Like the consensus seems to be that oldest children are generally less well-adjusted because they never get over the arrival of a younger sibling.
transcript.speaker: ED

transcript.text: Right, but on a positive note, some studies claimed that they were thought to be good at nurturing – certainly in the past when people had large families they would have been expected to look after the younger ones.
transcript.speaker: RUTH

transcript.text: There isn’t such a clear picture for middle children – but one trait that a lot of the studies mention is that they are easier to get on with than older or younger siblings.
transcript.speaker: ED

transcript.text: Generally eager to please and helpful – although that’s certainly not accurate as far as my family goes – my middle brother was a nightmare – always causing fights and envious of whatever I had.
transcript.speaker: RUTH

transcript.text: As I said – none of this seems to relate to my own experience. I’m the youngest in my family and I don’t recognise myself in any of the studies I’ve read about. I’m supposed to have been a sociable and confident child who made friends easily – but I was actually terribly shy.
transcript.speaker: ED

transcript.text: Really? That’s funny. There have been hundreds of studies on twins but mostly about nurture versus nature…
transcript.speaker: RUTH

transcript.text: There was one on personality, which said that a twin is likely to be quite shy in social situations because they always have their twin around to depend on for support.
transcript.speaker: ED

transcript.text: My cousins were like that when they were small – they were only interested in each other and found it hard to engage with other kids. They’re fine now though.
transcript.speaker: RUTH

transcript.text: Only children have had a really bad press – a lot of studies have branded them as loners who think the world revolves around them because they’ve never had to fight for their parents’ attention.
transcript.speaker: ED

transcript.text: That does seem a bit harsh. One category I hadn’t considered before was children with much older siblings – a couple of studies mentioned that these children grow up more quickly and are expected to do basic things for themselves – like getting dressed.
transcript.speaker: RUTH

transcript.text: I can see how that might be true – although I expect they’re sometimes the exact opposite – playing the baby role and clamouring for special treatment.
transcript.speaker: ED

transcript.text: What was the problem with most of these studies, do you think?
transcript.speaker: RUTH

transcript.text: I think it was because in a lot of cases data was collected from only one sibling per family, who rated him or herself and his or her siblings at the same time.
transcript.speaker: ED

transcript.text: Mmm. Some of the old research into the relationship between birth order and academic achievement has been proved to be accurate though. Performances in intelligence tests decline slightly from the eldest child to his or her younger siblings. This has been proved in lots of recent studies.
transcript.speaker: RUTH

transcript.text: Yes. Although what many of them didn’t take into consideration was family size. The more siblings there are, the likelier the family is to have a low socioeconomic status – which can also account for differences between siblings in academic performance.
transcript.speaker: ED

transcript.text: The oldest boy might be given more opportunities than his younger sisters, for example.
transcript.speaker: RUTH

transcript.text: Exactly.
transcript.speaker: ED

transcript.text: But the main reason for the marginally higher academic performance of oldest children is quite surprising, I think. It’s not only that they benefit intellectually from extra attention at a young age – which is what I would have expected. It’s that they benefit from being teachers for their younger siblings, by verbalising processes.
transcript.speaker: RUTH

transcript.text: Right, and this gives them status and confidence, which again contribute, in a small way, to better performance.
transcript.speaker: ED

transcript.text: So would you say sibling rivalry has been a useful thing for you?
transcript.speaker: ED

transcript.text: I think so – my younger brother was incredibly annoying and we fought a lot but I think this has made me a stronger person. I know how to defend myself. We had some terrible arguments and I would have died rather than apologise to him – but we had to put up with each other and most of the time we co-existed amicably enough.
transcript.speaker: RUTH

transcript.text: Yes, my situation was pretty similar. But I don’t think having two older brothers made me any less selfish – I was never prepared to let my brothers use any of my stuff …
transcript.speaker: ED

transcript.text: That’s perfectly normal, whereas …
transcript.speaker: RUTH

transcript.text: Today I’m going to talk about the eucalyptus tree.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This is a very common tree here in Australia, where it’s also sometimes called the gum tree.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: First I’m going to talk about why it’s important, then I’m going to describe some problems it faces at present.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Right, well the eucalyptus tree is an important tree for lots of reasons.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For example, it gives shelter to creatures like birds and bats, and these and other species also depend on it for food, particularly the nectar from its flowers.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So it supports biodiversity.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It’s useful to us humans too, because we can kill germs with a disinfectant made from oil extracted from eucalyptus leaves.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The eucalyptus grows all over Australia and the trees can live for up to four hundred years.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So it’s alarming that all across the country, numbers of eucalyptus are falling because the trees are dying off prematurely.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So what are the reasons for this?
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: One possible reason is disease.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: As far back as the 1970s the trees started getting a disease called Mundulla Yellows.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The trees’ leaves would gradually turn yellow, then the tree would die.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It wasn’t until 2004 that they found the cause of the problem was lime, or calcium hydroxide to give it its proper chemical name, which was being used in the construction of roads.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The lime was being washed away into the ground and affecting the roots of the eucalyptus trees nearby.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: What it was doing was preventing the trees from sucking up the iron they needed for healthy growth.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: When this was injected back into the affected trees, they immediately recovered.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But this problem only affected a relatively small number of trees.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: By 2000, huge numbers of eucalyptus were dying along Australia’s East Coast, of a disease known as Bell-miner Associated Die-back.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The bell-miner is a bird, and the disease seems to be common where there are high populations of bell-miners.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Again it’s the leaves of the trees that are affected.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: What happens is that insects settle on the leaves and eat their way round them, destroying them as they go, and at the same time they secrete a solution which has sugar in it.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The bell-miner birds really like this solution, and in order to get as much as possible, they keep away other creatures that might try to get it.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So these birds and insects flourish at the expense of other species, and eventually so much damage is done to the leaves that the tree dies.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But experts say that trees can start looking sick before any sign of Bell-miner Associated Die-back.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So it looks as if the problem might have another explanation.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: One possibility is that it’s to do with the huge bushfires that we have in Australia.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: A theory proposed over 40 years ago by ecologist William Jackson is that the frequency of bushfires in a particular region affects the type of vegetation that grows there.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: If there are very frequent bushfires in a region, this encourages grass to grow afterwards, while if the bushfires are rather less frequent, this results in the growth of eucalyptus forests.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So why is this?
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Why do fairly frequent bushfires actually support the growth of eucalyptus?
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Well, one reason is that the fire stops the growth of other species which would consume water needed by eucalyptus trees.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And there’s another reason.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: If these other quick-growing species of bushes and plants are allowed to proliferate, they harm the eucalyptus in another way, by affecting the composition of the soil, and removing nutrients from it.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So some bushfires are actually essential for the eucalyptus to survive as long as they are not too frequent.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In fact there’s evidence that Australia’s indigenous people practised regular burning of bush land for thousands of years before the arrival of the Europeans.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But since Europeans arrived on the continent, the number of bushfires has been strictly controlled.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Now scientists believe that this reduced frequency of bushfires to low levels has led to what’s known as ‘dry rainforest’, which seems an odd name as usually we associate tropical rainforest with wet conditions.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And what’s special about this type of rainforest?
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Well, unlike tropical rainforest which is a rich ecosystem, this type of ecosystem is usually a simple one.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It has very thick, dense vegetation, but not much variety of species.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The vegetation provides lots of shade, so one species that does find it ideal is the bell-miner bird, which builds its nests in the undergrowth there.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But again that’s not helpful for the eucalyptus tree.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
